title: Registers & Register Files
summary: The fastest storage tier a CPU has, and the architectural-vs-physical register distinction interviewers love to probe.

slides.markdown:
**Registers** are storage built directly into the CPU core — no bus, no cache lookup, just wires to the ALU. They're the fastest storage a program can touch, accessible in a single clock cycle.

That speed is exactly why there are so few of them: a typical ISA exposes only 16–32 **architectural registers**, versus gigabytes of RAM. More registers means more wiring and a bigger, slower register file to read from in one cycle — space and speed are in direct tension.

Compilers work hard to keep the "hot" values of a computation in registers, because every value that spills to memory costs orders of magnitude more time to access.

Most registers are **general-purpose** — the compiler can put any value in them (locals, temporaries, function arguments). But a handful are **special-purpose**, with a fixed meaning the hardware itself relies on:

- **PC (program counter)** — the address of the next instruction to fetch.
- **SP (stack pointer)** — the top of the current call stack.
- **Flags/status register** — condition bits (zero, carry, overflow, negative) set by arithmetic, read by conditional branches.

You can't repurpose the PC to hold a loop counter — the hardware itself reads and writes it every cycle for a very specific job.

A register file is a small, extremely fast array of storage cells with dedicated **read and write ports** — most designs support two reads and one write per cycle, matching a typical `add rd, rs1, rs2`.

![Register file with two read ports and one write port, addressed by register number](assets/register-file-ports.svg)

More ports means more simultaneous instructions can read/write registers per cycle — valuable for superscalar CPUs — but each extra port adds real silicon area and wiring, so port count is a deliberate design trade-off, not free.

assets.alt: Register file with two read ports and one write port, addressed by register number

slides.markdown:
How many architectural registers an ISA exposes is a real design decision with compiler consequences:

| | Fewer (x86: 16 GPRs) | More (RISC-V: 32, ARM64: 31) |
|---|---|---|
| Register pressure | Higher — more spilling to memory | Lower — more values stay in registers |
| Instruction encoding | Fewer bits needed to name a register | More bits needed per register field |
| Compiler complexity | Must be cleverer about allocation | More headroom, simpler allocation |

More architectural registers generally helps performance by reducing memory traffic, but it costs encoding space — one reason older, encoding-constrained ISAs settled for fewer.

slides.subTitle: Architectural vs physical registers
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "An x86-64 chip literally has exactly 16 general-purpose registers, full stop."

**Why it's wrong:** 16 is the count of **architectural registers** — the names the ISA exposes to software. Internally, modern out-of-order CPUs have hundreds of **physical registers** and use **register renaming** to map each architectural name onto a different physical one per use, avoiding false dependencies between instructions.

**Correct model:** architectural register count is fixed by the ISA (a software-visible contract); physical register count is a microarchitectural implementation detail that can differ chip to chip, just like cache size.

Register count is **fixed by the ISA**, not a free microarchitectural choice — every register instruction encodes a fixed-width field to name its registers, so the count is baked in the moment the encoding is finalized.

This is why RISC-V can't silently "add" more architectural registers in a later chip without breaking every existing binary — doing so would need a genuinely new ISA variant. Contrast this with cache size or pipeline depth, which a vendor can freely change between chip generations without touching software at all.
